title: Quantum Transport and Apparent Work Function Distributions of Atomic Contacts via a 3D-Printed High-Vacuum Platform
abstract: We present a low-cost, 3D-printed high-vacuum platform integrating a mechanically controllable break-junction system and a custom logarithmic amplifier for room-temperature quantum transport measurements. Using copper as a highly reactive test case, we successfully resolve the $1G_0$ conductance quantum under both high vacuum and anhydrous glycerol, demonstrating the effectiveness of these environments against rapid atmospheric oxidation. In parallel, utilizing gold as a robust benchmark, we systematically extract the apparent work function ($φ$) from thousands of tunneling traces across ambient air, vacuum, and glycerol. Our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of $φ$ rigorously follows a non-central chi-square distribution. The obtained gold work functions match existing literature across all environments. Although lower than bulk values, they perfectly align with theoretical models accounting for atomic-scale roughness, apex geometry, and environmental adsorbates. Ultimately, this methodology establishes an accessible and reproducible framework for systematic nanoscale research on reactive materials.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, low-cost 3D-printed platform for conducting room-temperature quantum transport measurements using break junctions. By analyzing conductance decay in the tunneling regime, the authors systematically extract the apparent work function ($\phi$) of contacts across different environments. This establishes an accessible and reproducible framework for nanoscale research on reactive materials.
main_problem: To develop an accessible, low-cost methodology for performing quantum transport measurements on reactive materials at room temperature.
main_result: The study successfully resolved the conductance quantum in highly reactive contacts and established that the apparent work function distribution follows a non-central chi-square distribution, matching theoretical predictions accounting for atomic roughness.
method: Measurements were performed using a custom 3D-printed break junction setup to characterize current decay (tunneling regime) across various environments (vacuum, glycerol).
model_or_system: The system uses a Mechanically Controllable Break Junction (MCBJ) housed in a PLA vacuum chamber. Quantum transport is analyzed using the Landauer formalism, relating conductance decay exponentially to the apparent work function ($\phi$).
key_observables: Conductance quantum ($G_0$), Apparent Work Function ($\phi$), Statistical distribution of $\phi$ (non-central chi-square).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, high vacuum capability ($1.4 	imes 10^{-4}$ mbar), and the dependence on environmental adsorbates.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes linearity in the tunneling regime for work function extraction and that the PLA platform is structurally sound for pressure differentials up to 1 atm.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate hardware setups, vacuum pump-down curves, conductance histograms showing $1G_0$ peaks across environments, and statistical fits of $\phi$ distributions using non-central chi-square models.
paper_structure: The paper details the low-cost experimental platform construction, presents measurements on reactive metals (Cu) in various atmospheres to test environmental robustness, and then uses Au as a benchmark to systematically extract and statistically analyze the apparent work function ($\phi$) from tunneling decay traces.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the rigorous statistical analysis of quantum transport signatures ($\phi$ distribution) provides valuable insights into surface physics and interface phenomena relevant to open quantum systems modeling.
